rationale: The declaration that God is good to those upright in heart corresponds to the prayer that the Lord do good to the good and upright in heart; one affirms what the other requests.
The speaker's almost-shaken feet correspond to the confession that a foot has been shaken and the Lord's mercy helps. Both place endangered footing within personal dependence on God.
The speaker admits envying lawless people when seeing their peace; the other psalm expressly forbids envy of evildoers and workers of lawlessness.

The claim that sinners escape human scourging corresponds to Job's complaint that the ungodly have flourishing houses without the Lord's scourge. This compares the complaints without treating prosperity as moral approval.
Arrogant people wrap themselves in injustice and ungodliness here; Psalm108 pictures a curse worn like a garment. Both make harmful moral conditions into clothing, while naming different conditions.

Speaking wickedness and injustice against the height corresponds to the horn's words against the Most High. The comparison concerns hostile speech, without identifying the psalm's sinners as Daniel's king.
The sinners ask whether the Most High knows; Psalm93 reports the claim that the Lord neither sees nor understands and answers it through God's making human faculties of perception.
Both complaints explicitly place ungodly people alongside continued life or prosperity and accumulated wealth, challenging an uncomplicated equation between present riches and righteousness.
Washing hands among the innocent repeats the other psalm's wording. Here the speaker questions its value; there washing accompanies approaching the Lord's altar.

The speaker calls his righteous conduct vain while observing prosperous sinners; Malachi reports people calling service to God futile and lawbreakers blessed. Both voice a complaint that their wider contexts examine.
Trying to understand the apparent prosperity of sinners becomes toil for the psalmist. Ecclesiastes likewise joins the effort to understand God's works with toil and the limits of human discovery.
The psalm describes those lifted up being cast down; Mary's song describes proud people scattered and rulers brought down from thrones. The comparison preserves the different groups and settings.

The sinners' sudden desolation corresponds to Zophar's description of the ungodly perishing when they think themselves established. This compares the stated reversal without endorsing Zophar's application to Job.

The sinners' image becomes worthless like a dream on awakening; Zophar likewise pictures the ungodly disappearing like a dream or nighttime apparition. The shared image does not establish his accusation against Job.

Both passages compare threatening wealth or appearances with dreams emptied of substance on waking. Isaiah explicitly describes nations attacking Jerusalem, while the psalm places the divine dismissal in God's city.

The speaker admits not understanding and becoming beastlike beside God; Psalm48 compares an honored but uncomprehending person to senseless beasts. The self-confession and general warning retain their different scopes.
The testimony that God grasped the speaker's right hand corresponds to God's promise to hold Israel's right hand and tell it not to fear.

relationship: Reception by God amid the wealth question
rationale: The speaker says God received him with glory; Psalm48 anticipates God's receiving and redeeming the soul from Hades. Both occur in reflections on riches and mortality, with different temporal wording.
The failing speaker identifies God as his enduring portion; Psalm15 explicitly calls the Lord the portion of the speaker's inheritance and cup. The shared possession language concerns God Himself.
Going whoring away from God corresponds to Hosea's description of the land prostituting itself away from following the Lord. Both use marital infidelity to describe religious departure.
The resolution to proclaim all God's praises in the gates of daughter Zion repeats the same specific proclamation and location in Psalm9.
The lament addresses divine anger against the sheep of God's pasture; Psalm99 identifies the community as His people and the sheep of His pasture, supplying the same communal flock description.
The prayer recalls God's acquired and redeemed congregation and His dwelling at Zion. Exodus15 combines the purchased people, the mountain of inheritance and God's prepared sanctuary.

The plea focuses on evil done by an enemy in God's holy places; Lamentations describes the sanctuary's rejection and an enemy's shout within the Lord's house. The parallel does not settle the psalm's date.

relationship: Enemy noise in a sacred feast setting
rationale: Enemies boast inside God's feast here; Lamentations depicts a shout in the Lord's house as on a festival day. The correspondence concerns hostile occupation of a sacred celebration setting.

The psalm describes doors cut down with tools; Maccabees describes burned gates and demolished sanctuary chambers. These are concrete sanctuary-ruin parallels, with different destructive methods and no asserted single occasion.

The complaint that enemies burned God's sanctuary corresponds to the narrative of the Babylonian chief cook setting the Lord's house and Jerusalem's houses on fire. This is a historical counterpart, not a dating claim.
The enemy wishes to burn God's feasts from the earth; Lamentations laments the destruction of festival and Sabbath in Zion. The agents and the wish-versus-description forms remain distinct.

The absence of a prophet or signs corresponds to the lament that Zion's prophets saw no vision from the Lord. The texts describe deprivation of prophetic guidance without supplying an identical historical date.
The psalm asks how long the adversary will reproach God's name; the oracle against the Assyrian king identifies his reproach and blasphemy as directed against Israel's Holy One.

relationship: Withdrawal of the divine right hand
rationale: The lament asks why God's right hand is withdrawn; Lamentations expressly says He turned back His right hand before the enemy. Both describe withheld protection through this bodily image.
The confession of God's ancient kingship and saving work corresponds to the sea song's account of redeemed people led to the sanctuary and its affirmation that the Lord reigns for ever.

The psalm depicts God crushing dragons' heads on water; Isaiah depicts God killing a dragon with His powerful sword. The comparison concerns divine victory over dragon imagery, without identifying each creature.

Both passages picture God's overthrow of a dragon followed by its being given as food. Ezekiel names Pharaoh and animal or bird consumers; the psalm names Ethiopian peoples as recipients. The dragon identities are not equated.

relationship: Miraculous control of rivers and springs
rationale: Both poems combine retreating or dried waters with waters opened as springs. Psalm113 names the Jordan and a rock; Psalm73 names rivers of Etham. Those names and images are preserved, not equated.

relationship: Creation of day and night lights
rationale: The declaration that day and night belong to God and that He fashioned light and sun corresponds to God's making and appointing the heavenly lights to govern day and night.

Summer and spring shaped by God correspond to the post-flood assurance that summer and spring will not cease. Both retain this edition's season names rather than substituting another translation's wording.
The request to remember the enemy's reproach and provocation of God's name returns to verse10's question about the adversary reproaching that name, renewing the appeal after the creation imagery.
The plea not to forget needy souls corresponds to the assurance that the poor will not be utterly forgotten and the needy person's endurance will not perish for ever.

The plea that God look upon His covenant during violence corresponds to the covenant assurances that He will remember the ancestral covenant and not dissolve it even while His people are in their enemies' land.

relationship: Praise joined to the poor's relief
rationale: The humbled and needy are expected to praise God's name here. Psalm68 joins praise of that name with the poor's rejoicing and the assurance that the Lord hears the needy.

The appeal that God arise and judge His case corresponds to Micah's announcement that the Lord has a case to argue. Micah names Israel as the opposing party; the psalm's hostile reproachers are not thereby equated with Israel.

The enemies' arrogance ascends continually toward God; the Assyrian oracle likewise says the king's arrogance rose to God's ears. The shared upward image specifies divine awareness of hostile arrogance.
Both headings contain the instruction Do not destroy. Their named authors and additional heading information differ, so this does not identify a tune or equate their occasions.
Acknowledging God and calling upon His name corresponds to the command to give thanks to the Lord and call upon His name. Both join thanksgiving to this act of invocation.

The psalm associates an appointed time with judging uprightness; Paul describes a fixed day for judging the world in righteousness. This formal correspondence does not identify the psalm's first-person speaker with Paul's appointed Man.
The psalm contrasts the melting earth with established pillars; Job describes God shaking the earth so that its pillars sway. Both use earth-pillars imagery, with opposite stability conditions.
The warning against lawlessness and raising a horn corresponds to Hannah's warning not to boast or speak loftily. Each opposes self-exaltation in the setting of God's power to reverse human standing.
The command not to lift the horn high or speak injustice against God corresponds to the prohibition of lofty and grandiose speech in Hannah's prayer. The horn image remains the psalm's own wording.
God's humbling one and raising another closely corresponds to Hannah's declaration that the Lord humbles and raises high, explicitly placing reversals of standing in His hands.

relationship: The Lord's cup of punitive wine
rationale: Both passages place a cup of unmixed wine in the Lord's hand and make nations or sinners drink it. The psalm's mixture and dregs details are retained rather than harmonized with Jeremiah.

relationship: Cup of anger passed to oppressors
rationale: The Lord's cup drunk by sinners corresponds to Isaiah's cup of anger taken from Jerusalem and given to her oppressors. Isaiah supplies a transfer between groups, rather than the psalm's precise dregs description.
The promise to exult and sing to the God of Jacob corresponds to the invitation to exult and shout to the God of Jacob. The first is a personal pledge; the second calls a community to praise.

The righteous person's raised horn contrasts with broken sinners' horns; Hannah's prayer similarly combines opponents' weakening with the raising of the horn of God's anointed. The righteous figure and anointed are not assumed identical.

God's being known in Judea and His great name in Israel corresponds to the declaration of His word and judgments to Israel in a way not given to other nations. The latter specifies the disclosure's content.
The placement of God's dwelling in Zion corresponds to the explicit declaration that He chose Zion as His dwelling and enduring resting place.
Both passages describe the breaking of bows and weapons by God in the ending or defeat of war. Psalm75 locates the action in His dwelling's setting; Psalm45 gives it an earth-wide horizon.

The light from everlasting mountains corresponds to the Holy One's coming from a shaded mountain with brightness like light. The descriptions retain their different mountain qualities and temporal wording.

The drowsiness of mounted warriors at God's rebuke corresponds to the sea song's overthrow of horse and rider. This compares poetic depictions of mounted military power disabled by God, not identical methods or events.
Both passages ask who can stand before God's anger, making the inability to resist His wrath the explicit rhetorical question.
God arises to save the earth's meek; Isaiah's Jesse-root figure judges the cause of the lowly of the earth. The shared judicial concern for the lowly does not collapse the two acting figures.
The call to make and repay vows to the Lord corresponds to the law requiring a vow to the Lord to be paid without delay. The law also specifies liability for failure.

relationship: Divine withdrawal of spirit or breath
rationale: God takes away rulers' spirits here; Psalm103 describes Him taking creatures' breath so that they fail and return to dust. The correspondence preserves the rulers-versus-creatures scope and different English nouns.
Both headings say For the end and concerning Jeduthun. Asaph and David remain their different named authors; no identification with differently spelled Chronicles names is required.
Both lines say that the speaker cried to the Lord with his voice and received divine attention or hearing. Psalm3 adds the holy mountain as the place of response.

The soul's refusal to be comforted corresponds to Jacob's refusal of his family's comfort while mourning Joseph. The comparison concerns the refusal itself, not an identification of the psalmist's loss.

The movement between remembering God and a fainting spirit corresponds to Psalm142's despondent spirit followed by remembering ancient days and God's works. The psalms order these responses differently.
Eyes anticipating the watches correspond to eyes awake before dawn for meditation on God's sayings. The troubled silence here remains distinct from the target's expressly stated meditation purpose.
The speaker considers ancient days and everlasting years; Moses commands remembering old days and considering successive generations' years, directing remembrance toward inherited testimony.
Speaking at night with one's heart corresponds to the instruction to speak in one's heart upon one's bed. Searching reflection here and remorse in the target are kept distinct.
The question whether the Lord rejects for the ages corresponds to the assurance that He will not reject for ever and will have compassion after humbling.
The question whether mercy will be cut off for ever corresponds to the promise contrasting brief abandonment and anger with everlasting mercy and an enduring covenant of peace.
The question whether God forgets to show pity corresponds to Zion's complaint of being forgotten and God's answer that even if a mother forgets, He will not forget Zion.
The question whether wrath shuts divine compassion corresponds to Habakkuk's statement that in wrath God will remember mercy. The different interrogative and affirming forms remain explicit.
The resolve to remember the Lord's works and original wonders corresponds to the command to remember His wonders, portents and judgments.
Meditating on all God's works closely repeats the combination of remembering, meditating on all His works and pondering the work of His hands in Psalm142.
The question what god is great like Israel's God corresponds to the sea song's question who is like the Lord among the gods, glorious among the holy ones and working wonders.

relationship: Wonders revealing divine power to peoples
rationale: The declaration that God makes His power known among peoples through wonders corresponds to the promised signs in Egypt through which the Egyptians will know the Lord.
Redeeming the people with God's arm corresponds to the promise to ransom Israel from Egyptian slavery with an uplifted arm and great judgment.
The waters see God and fear here; Psalm113 personifies the sea as seeing and fleeing, then places the earth's trembling before the God of Jacob.

God's arrows passing through the sounding clouds correspond to Habakkuk's divine missiles and flashing weapons moving into light. The comparison concerns the theophany's weapon imagery, not identical weather details.

The thunderous divine voice, lightning and trembling earth correspond to Psalm17's heavenly thunder, multiplied lightning and exposed foundations at God's rebuke. The wheel remains this psalm's distinct wording.

The divine way and paths through waters correspond to the sea being divided and Israel walking through its midst on dry ground. Exodus describes the passage, without stating the psalm's hidden-tracks image.

relationship: Moses and Aaron in the Exodus leadership
rationale: The people guided by the hands of Moses and Aaron correspond to God's statement that He brought Israel from Egypt and sent Moses, Aaron and Miriam before them. Micah names an additional leader.
The address asking God's people to attend to His law corresponds to Moses' call for Israel to hear the ordinances and judgments and learn to perform them.

Matthew introduces as prophetic Scripture the words about opening the mouth in parables and uttering things hidden from the foundation. These correspond to the psalm's parables and original enigmas, with its wording preserved.
What the community heard and learned from its fathers corresponds to Moses' instruction to ask fathers and elders about ancient days so that they will tell the next generation.

relationship: Transmission of divine works to children
rationale: The promise to recount God's strength and wonders to the next generation corresponds to the command not to forget what Israel saw and to make it known to sons and sons' sons.
God's established testimony and law are given for fathers to teach their sons; Deuteronomy expressly commands impressing these words on one's children.

The psalm's children rising to announce the testimony to their own children corresponds to instruction addressed to parents to teach their children, followed by a promise concerning the days of both parents and children.
The purpose is to avoid forgetting God's works and to seek His commandments; Deuteronomy likewise warns against forgetting the witnessed works or letting them depart from the heart.
The crooked and provoking generation whose spirit is not faithful corresponds to Moses' address to a crooked generation that fails to respond rightly to its Father and maker.
The psalm joins failure to keep God's covenant with refusal of His law; Hosea joins transgressing His covenant with acting impiously against His law.
The people forget God's benefits and displayed wonders here; Psalm105 says they quickly forgot His works instead of awaiting His counsel.
The wonders before Israel's fathers in Egypt correspond to God's promised multiplication of signs and portents in Egypt. Exodus does not name the psalm's specific plain of Tanis.
The psalm recounts God splitting the sea and taking the people through; Exodus narrates the divided waters and Israel's passage on dry ground. Skin-bag and wall descriptions remain distinct images.
Daytime guidance by cloud and nighttime guidance by fiery light correspond directly to the pillar of cloud by day and pillar of fire by night leading Israel.

relationship: Water from rock in the wilderness
rationale: The psalm's split rock supplying drink in the wilderness corresponds to the command to strike the rock at Horeb so water will come out for the people to drink.

Paul speaks of the ancestors drinking from the accompanying spiritual rock and identifies that rock as Christ. This is an explicit later interpretation alongside the psalm's water-giving rock, not an explicit Christ-name in the psalm.

The picture of water brought from rock in torrents corresponds to Moses striking the rock and abundant water flowing for the congregation and its animals. This compares the water provision without merging the two wilderness rock narratives.
The continued sin and provocation in a waterless place correspond to the congregation's bitter dispute with Moses and Aaron over the wilderness lacking water and food-producing land.
Testing God by asking food for their cravings corresponds to the mixed crowd and Israel craving food and weeping for meat rather than being satisfied with manna.
Psalm105 explicitly links a craving for desire in the wilderness to testing God in a waterless place, closely combining the same acts as this verse.

The people's question whether God can prepare a wilderness table corresponds to Moses asking how the immense people can be supplied with meat. The speakers differ, and God's reply challenges the supposed limit on His hand.

The question whether God can give bread after providing rock-water is answered by comparison with His explicit promise to rain bread from heaven for the people. Exodus is a narrative counterpart, not a quoted answer to this line.

relationship: Complaint heard and answered with fire
rationale: Numbers recounts the Lord hearing a complaint, becoming angry and kindling fire among the people. The psalm likewise connects His hearing with fire and wrath, while retaining its intervening statement that He delayed.
The psalm explains the judgment through unbelief in God; Moses likewise accuses Israel of disobeying the command to enter the land and not believing Him or listening to His voice.

Opening heaven's doors for the ensuing manna contrasts with the officer's disbelief that promised food abundance could happen even if the Lord made openings in heaven. The wilderness and besieged-city events remain distinct.
The raining of manna as heaven's bread corresponds to God's promise to rain bread from heaven, retaining the same provision and directional imagery.

relationship: Citation and interpretation of heavenly bread
rationale: John's speakers cite the giving of bread from heaven while discussing their fathers' manna; Jesus then distinguishes the Father-given true bread. This provides an explicit later citation and interpretation of the shared bread language.
The angels' bread eaten by people corresponds to Wisdom's account of God's feeding His people with angels' food and providing bread from heaven, elaborating the gift's sweetness and adaptability.
Numbers describes a wind from the Lord bringing quails from the sea. It supports the food-bearing divine wind context, while not supplying the psalm's south and southwest compass directions.
The raining of flesh and winged birds in immense numbers corresponds to the quails spread in abundance around the camp and gathered by the people.
The birds fall amid the camp and around its tents; Numbers likewise places the quails all around the camp and describes the people's gathering and spreading them there.

The people's eating and receiving their desire corresponds to God's announced granting of the meat they demanded. Numbers also makes the gift a judgment, so satisfaction is not treated as divine approval of the craving.
The food is still in the people's mouth before the psalm's next judgment; Numbers places the onset of divine anger while the meat is still between their teeth.
The deadly anger during the food episode corresponds to the great plague and burial of the people who craved. The psalm's particular description of the victims remains its own wording.
Continued unbelief after the wonders corresponds to God's question how long the people will refuse to believe Him despite all the signs He performed among them.
The wasting of their days and years corresponds to the judgment that the rebellious adults' bodies will fall in the wilderness and their children will bear the prolonged wandering.

relationship: Death followed by turning to God
rationale: The people seek God when He kills among them; Numbers narrates deaths from the serpents followed by confession of sin and a request that Moses pray to the Lord.
Remembering the Most High as their redeemer corresponds to His promise to free and ransom the sons of Israel from Egyptian bondage.
The people love with the mouth and lie with the tongue here; Isaiah exposes mouth and lip honor while the heart remains far away. The psalm's next line similarly diagnoses the heart.
The unstraight heart and unfaithfulness to covenant correspond to Moses' description of a perverse generation and sons without faithfulness.
Mercy, expiation and repeated restraint of anger correspond to the confession that the Lord is compassionate, slow to anger and does not deal with people according to their sins.
God remembers that the people are flesh and a departing breath; Psalm102 says He remembers human dust and compares mortal flourishing with grass ended by a passing spirit or wind.
The repeated provocation in the wilderness corresponds to Moses' list of places where Israel provoked the Lord and his conclusion that they remained disobedient.
The repeated testing of God corresponds to His statement that those who saw His glory and signs in Egypt and the wilderness tested Him ten times and did not listen.

The people fail to remember the hand that ransomed them from affliction; Exodus places God's covenant remembrance alongside His promise to ransom them from Egyptian slavery. The remembering parties differ.
God's setting signs and portents in Egypt corresponds to His announced multiplication of signs and portents there. The plain of Tanis remains a location named only in the psalm's description.
The turning of water into blood so people cannot drink corresponds to the Nile becoming blood, fish dying and Egyptians being unable to drink its water.
The dogfly that consumes the people corresponds to the grievous dogfly entering Pharaoh's house and his servants' houses and ruining the land.
The frog that ruins the Egyptians corresponds to Aaron extending his hand over the waters and frogs coming up to cover Egypt's land. This is the verse's other separately named plague.
The handing of labor's fruit to locusts corresponds to the locusts consuming the land's vegetation and remaining tree fruit. The separate mildew named in the psalm is not relabeled as locusts.

The striking of vines with hail corresponds to the hail's destruction of field vegetation and trees. The psalm's additional frost upon sycamores is retained without claiming Exodus supplies that detail.

relationship: Hail and fire against livestock and property
rationale: The cattle delivered to hail and possessions to fire correspond to the hail with flashing fire striking people, livestock and plants in the field.

Within the Egyptian plague account, the psalm describes a mission through evil angels; Exodus mentions the destroyer barred from marked Israelite houses. Both describe destructive agency in that judgment, without equating the plural angels with the singular destroyer.

The beasts shut up in death correspond to the announced deadly plague upon Egyptian livestock and its execution. This retains the psalm's animal clause rather than substituting an account solely of human deaths.
The smiting of every firstborn in Egypt corresponds directly to the midnight striking of Egyptian firstborn from Pharaoh's house to the captive, together with livestock firstborn.
Both psalms describe God guiding His people like sheep. Psalm76 names Moses and Aaron as the means; Psalm77 places this flock-leading in the wilderness after Egypt's judgment.
The people's secure leading and their enemies' covering by the sea correspond to Israel crossing safely while the waters cover Pharaoh's forces, followed by Israel's trust in the Lord.
Bringing the people to the holy mountain acquired by God's right hand corresponds to the sea song's anticipation of bringing and planting them on God's inheritance mountain and prepared sanctuary.
The dispossession of nations and allocation of land to Israel's tribes correspond to Joshua's taking the land and giving it as an inheritance divided among their tribes.
The refusal to keep God's testimonies after land settlement corresponds to Judges' account of Israel doing evil, abandoning the Lord and turning to the surrounding peoples' gods.

The people's turning aside like a crooked bow corresponds to Hosea's turning-away charge and bow comparison. This edition calls Hosea's bow drawn, not crooked; the image is related without claiming identical wording.
Provocation through high places and jealousy through carved images correspond to Moses' description of Israel provoking God with foreign gods and abominations, followed by His jealous anger.
God hears and rejects Israel here; Jeremiah describes ignored divine speech followed by rejection from His presence, explicitly recalling Ephraim's rejection.
The rejection of the tent at Shiloh corresponds to God's instruction to consider what He did to Shiloh, where His name had first dwelt, because of Israel's evil.

relationship: Captured glory in the Shiloh narrative
rationale: Power and beauty are handed to enemies in the psalm's Shiloh context; Samuel narrates the ark's capture and the declaration that glory departed from Israel. This is a contextual literary correspondence, not a replacement of the psalm's nouns with ark.
The handing of God's people to the sword corresponds to Israel's defeat and the great slaughter in the battle that precedes the ark's capture.

relationship: Deaths of the priests in the ark battle
rationale: The priests falling by the sword correspond to the deaths of Hophni and Phinehas when the ark was taken; their priestly office is supplied in 1Samuel1:3. Samuel does not expressly state the psalm's unweeping-widows detail.

relationship: Awakening imagery addressed to the Lord
rationale: The Lord's rising as from sleep corresponds to the plea that He awaken and the question why He sleeps. Both use sleep imagery for divine apparent inactivity; the heavy-with-wine simile belongs only to Psalm77.
The refusal to choose Ephraim's tribe corresponds to God's explicit statement that He rejected all Ephraim's seed. The psalm additionally names Joseph's tent.
God's choice of Judah corresponds to David's explanation that the Lord chose Judah for royal rule. Chronicles narrows the purpose to kingship, while the psalm continues into Zion's choice.
The choice and love of Mount Zion correspond to the declaration that the Lord chose Zion and desired her for His dwelling.

The sanctuary built with enduring establishment corresponds to God's consecration of Solomon's house with His name there for ever. The one-horned-beasts comparison is preserved without being reinterpreted as heights or architectural features.
God chooses David and takes him from sheepfolds here; Samuel narrates the youngest son being fetched from tending sheep and anointed in the midst of his brothers.
David is brought from following the nursing flock to shepherd God's people; God's oracle says He took David from the sheepfold, from following the flock, to become ruler over His people Israel.
The task of shepherding Jacob and Israel corresponds to the Lord's reported command that David shepherd His people Israel and become their ruler.

David shepherds with an innocent heart and skill here; God's instruction to Solomon cites David's conduct with holiness of heart and uprightness. The practical skill clause remains a distinct psalm detail.

The lament over the holy temple's defilement corresponds to the inspection of a desolate sanctuary, profaned altar and burned gates. The correspondence does not establish that both texts describe the same invasion.

relationship: Zion reduced to a watcher's shelter
rationale: Jerusalem's becoming a fruit-watchman's hut corresponds to daughter Zion left as a fruit-watcher's shelter and a besieged city. Both use an exposed agricultural shelter for the city's diminished condition.

relationship: Corpses left to birds and beasts
rationale: The servants' bodies and holy ones' flesh given to birds and beasts correspond to Jeremiah's warning that the people's corpses will become food for heaven's birds and earth's beasts.
Maccabees explicitly introduces as Scripture the handing over of God's holy ones' flesh, joining this verse's wording to the bloodshed and absent burial of the next verse.
Maccabees quotes the pouring of blood around Jerusalem with no one to bury, applying the psalm's distinctive language to the killing narrated there.
Both verses describe becoming a reproach to neighbors and a mockery and derision to those around, repeating the same communal humiliation formula.
Both laments ask How long of the Lord, speak of persistence to the end and compare divine anger with blazing fire. Jealousy here and wrath in Psalm88 retain their distinct wording.

relationship: Close verbal parallel in the wrath petition
rationale: Both ask God to pour wrath on peoples that do not know Him and communities that do not call on His name. The psalm's kingdoms and Jeremiah's generations remain distinct labels.
Both explain the petition by saying the enemies consumed Jacob and desolated his place, linking the plea for judgment to the same named victim and devastation.

relationship: Selective remembrance of mercy and sins
rationale: The plea not to remember ancient lawlessness and to bring compassion corresponds to the request to remember ancient mercies rather than the speaker's youthful sins. The communal and personal confessions remain distinct.

relationship: Forgiveness and God's reputation among nations
rationale: The appeal for rescue and expiation for God's name corresponds to Moses' appeal concerning what foreign nations will say, followed by his request to forgive the people's sin according to great mercy.
The question why nations should ask where Israel's God is repeats the challenge in Psalm113, whose preceding appeal likewise concerns God's name, mercy and truth.

relationship: Prisoners' groans and those marked for death
rationale: Both passages combine the groan of bound people with concern for the sons of those put to death. One petitions for their preservation; the other describes God's hearing and release.

The requested sevenfold repayment for neighbors' reproach corresponds to the law's sevenfold punishment for Israel's sins. The numerical punishment pattern is shared, while the recipients differ and the law is not presented as an instruction for the psalmist's appeal.
The community calls itself God's people and pasture sheep and pledges praise; Psalm99 uses that same communal identification and proceeds to thanksgiving and praise of His enduring goodness.
Both headings include concerning those who will be changed. Their other directions and historical notices differ; this correspondence does not identify the Assyrian occasion of Psalm79.
The appeal to the One seated upon the cherubim corresponds to the description of the Lord associated with the covenant ark and seated upon the cherubim.

Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh form the prayer's named group; Numbers places Manasseh and Benjamin in the camp formation led by Ephraim. This explains a concrete tribal grouping without dating the psalm to the march.

relationship: The divine face shining for favor
rationale: The plea that God's face appear brightly so the people will be saved corresponds to the priestly blessing asking Him to make His face shine upon the recipient and show mercy.

The psalm asks how long God will be angry against His servants' prayer; Lamentations describes crying out and calling while God blocks the prayer. Both lament prayer itself encountering divine opposition.
The bread of tears and abundant drink of tears correspond to the personal lament that tears became the speaker's bread day and night. The drinking image is an additional feature here.
The neighbors' reproach and enemies' mockery correspond to the same communal humiliation by neighbors and surrounding people in Psalm43.
The request to turn the people back and make God's face shine so they will be saved repeats verse4 after the tear-food and enemy-ridicule complaints, now adding powers to God's title.

relationship: Nations displaced and a people planted
rationale: The vine transplanted from Egypt after nations are cast out corresponds to Psalm43's statement that God's hand destroyed nations and planted the ancestors. The planting metaphor carries the people's settlement in both.

The vine's rooting and filling the land corresponds to Jeremiah's description of people planted by God, taking root and producing growth. Jeremiah speaks of prosperous wicked people, not the psalm's collective vine identity.

relationship: Extent described by sea and river
rationale: The vine's branches reaching sea and river correspond to Israel's promised boundaries running to the sea and river. The psalm's unnamed bodies of water are not assigned more precise identities than its text supplies.
The question why God tore down the vine's fence so passersby plunder it corresponds to His announced removal of His vineyard's fence so it becomes spoil and is trampled.

relationship: Appeal to look down from heaven
rationale: The request that God turn back, look from heaven and see corresponds to Isaiah's appeal that He turn from heaven and see from His holy dwelling amid a complaint about withheld compassion.

The son of man whom God strengthened for Himself recurs with the same wording in verse18, where he is paired with the man of God's right hand. The repetition is recorded without settling the figure's identity.

The vine's burning in the psalm corresponds to the gathering and burning of branches in Jesus' vine discourse. The collective vine here and branches failing to abide in Jesus are different referents and explanations.
The petition for God's hand upon the man of His right hand repeats verse16's son-of-man clause, connecting the two petitions without identifying that person as a particular king or as Christ.

relationship: Renewed communal life and response to God
rationale: The appeal that God give life so the people call on His name corresponds to the question whether He will turn and give them life so His people rejoice in Him. The promised responses differ but both follow communal renewal.
The final appeal repeats verse4's turning, shining face and salvation clauses, closing the vine petitions with the fuller title Lord God of powers.
Both headings give the direction For the end, concerning the winepresses. Their named authors differ, and the heading's musical or historical meaning is not inferred.
Both openings invite exultation in the Lord or God and a shout to God as helper or Savior. The God-of-Jacob title is an additional specification in Psalm80.
The command to sound the tambourine and psaltery corresponds to praise of God's name with tambourine and psaltery. The lyre additionally named here is not supplied by the target.

relationship: Trumpets at new moons and festivals
rationale: The trumpet at the new moon and feast corresponds to the ordinance to sound trumpets on feast days and new moons, giving the same specific ceremonial occasions.

Calling the preceding trumpet observance an ordinance for Israel corresponds to the divine instruction commanding trumpets at new moons and feasts as a memorial before God. The connection depends on the read verse4 context.
The removal of the back from burdens corresponds to God's promise to bring Israel out from Egyptian oppression and slavery. The psalm's basket work remains its more particular labor image.

The psalm names God's testing at the water of contention; Numbers identifies the water of contention as where Israel reviled the Lord and He was sanctified among them. The parties' different actions are not exchanged or harmonized.
God's address Hear, My people, Israel corresponds to Moses' summons for Israel to hear the statutes and judgments, in each case introducing covenant instruction.

relationship: Prohibition of other gods and their worship
rationale: The ban on a new or foreign god and bowing to one corresponds to the Decalogue's prohibition of other gods and bowing to or serving their images.

The Lord identifies Himself as Israel's God who brought it from Egypt, corresponding directly to the Decalogue's opening self-identification. The promise to fill an opened mouth is the psalm's additional wording.

relationship: Divine speech met by refusal to listen
rationale: Israel's not listening to God's voice corresponds to His complaint that He repeatedly spoke and called but the people did not listen or answer.

relationship: God handing people over to their desires
rationale: Sending the people away according to their hearts' practices corresponds to God's handing people over in their hearts' desires. The communities and specified subsequent conduct differ.

relationship: Unrealized blessing after refusal to listen
rationale: The conditional lament If My people had listened corresponds to Isaiah's If you had listened to My commandments, followed in both contexts by blessings that would have followed obedience.

relationship: Defeat of enemies under the obedience promise
rationale: God would have humbled Israel's enemies under the preceding obedience condition; Deuteronomy's blessing for obedience likewise promises that the Lord will hand opposing enemies over to be crushed.

relationship: Honey from rock and finest wheat
rationale: Both passages combine honey supplied from rock with the finest wheat, preserving the distinctive pair of provisions rather than linking only generic food abundance.
